open_obligations: Check that grade-school math is 'more challenging' in the sense Anil et al. mean, given it has known answers.
Note that Kirchner et al. use a role-conditioned helpful/sneaky prover, not Anil et al.'s single prover that always argues for label 1.
Check how far from equilibrium the trained players are, since no equilibrium guarantee is given.
out.other_title: Open questions: scaling PVGs to harder problems and behaviour at approximate equilibria
out.rationale: Anil et al. call for scaling PVGs to harder problems and studying behaviour at approximate equilibria. Kirchner et al. train GPT-4-family helpful and sneaky provers against much smaller verifiers on GSM and report rising helpful-prover accuracy, verifier robustness and human legibility; they train by coordinate descent toward an approximate local equilibrium and state the theory's prover-class assumption is not met.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether prover-verifier game training scales beyond toy tasks to LLMs trained toward approximate equilibria, on grade-school math

open_obligations: Note that Bai et al.'s concern is the AI feedback model's decisions, while Kirchner et al. study the policy's solutions.
Check whether legibility to small verifiers transfers to humans beyond grade-school math.
Note the legibility tax relative to correctness-only RL.
out.other_title: Scaling supervision risks automating and obscuring decision making
out.rationale: Bai et al. warn that scaling supervision may automate and obscure decision making and rely on chain-of-thought for legibility. Kirchner et al. report that optimising only for answer correctness makes solutions less legible to time-limited humans, and that prover-verifier checkability training restores legibility with a legibility tax; the concern is solution legibility in math, not the legibility of an AI supervisor's decisions.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether training can keep model reasoning legible to overseers rather than obscuring it, for chain-of-thought math solutions

text: The authors show that optimizing chain-of-thought solutions to grade-school math only for answer correctness can make them less legible, and propose a training algorithm inspired by Anil et al.'s Prover-Verifier Game that iteratively trains small verifiers to predict correctness, 'helpful' provers to produce correct solutions the verifier accepts, and 'sneaky' provers to produce incorrect solutions that fool it. They report that helpful-prover accuracy and verifier robustness increase over training, and that over training human accuracy rises when checking helpful-prover solutions and falls when checking sneaky-prover solutions.
title: Prover-verifier games (checkability training) improve legibility of LLM math solutions
